title: The Rise of Islam and the Abbasid Golden Age

cards.h: From a desert town to the world's best library in 200 years
cards.b:
In about 610 CE, a merchant of Mecca named Muhammad began to preach. Within a century, an Arabic-speaking empire stretched from Spain to Sindh.

How did this happen so fast? And what did it do with the world's books once it got them?

Muhammad (about 570-632 CE) taught belief in one God. After conflict in Mecca, he moved to Medina in 622 CE, the Hijra. That year begins the Islamic calendar. By his death most of Arabia was united.

The next leaders, the Rashidun caliphs, conquered Syria, Egypt and Persia in about 30 years. The Persian and Byzantine empires were exhausted from wars with each other.

The Umayyad caliphate (661-750) ruled from Damascus. Arabs held top posts, and non-Arab converts resented it. In 750 the Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads, with strong support from Persian-speaking eastern regions. One Umayyad prince escaped and founded a state in Spain.
Caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad in 762 as a round city on the Tigris. It became one of the largest cities in the world, with a paper industry (the craft came from China) feeding its book markets.

Al-Khwarizmi (about 780-850) wrote a book on al-jabr, giving us 'algebra'. His name gives us 'algorithm'. Ibn al-Haytham (about 965-1040) did experiments on light and sight. Al-Razi wrote on medicine. Al-Biruni studied India.

The House of Wisdom in Baghdad is famous as a great library and translation centre. Historians disagree on how formal it really was.

cards.h: The end of the golden age
cards.b:
Abbasid power weakened as regional rulers took over. In 1258, the Mongol army of Hulagu sacked Baghdad and killed the last Abbasid caliph. Many people died; estimates vary widely.

But Islamic science and culture lived on in Cairo, Cordoba, Samarkand and later in Istanbul and Delhi.

cards.h: Did the Tigris run black with ink?
cards.b: Myth: in 1258 the Tigris ran black with the ink of books thrown in by the Mongols, and red with blood.Fact: this poetic image comes from later writers. Baghdad's libraries were badly damaged, but exact details are uncertain. Also, 'Arabic numerals' are a misnomer: Arabs got them from India.

Five things to remember

  1. Hijra in 622 marks year one of the Islamic calendar.
  2. The Umayyads (661-750) ruled from Damascus; the Abbasids from Baghdad.
  3. Baghdad's scholars saved and extended world knowledge.
  4. Al-Khwarizmi gave us algebra and algorithm.
  5. The Mongols took Baghdad in 1258.

Think about it

  • What makes a city a centre of knowledge?
  • Who deserves credit for an idea that travels through many hands?
